country.comment: Case study of the city of Bukavu (communes of Bagira, Ibanda, and Kadutu) in South Kivu Province, eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo.
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Affiliations, and Abstract; PDF p. 3, Section 2.1.1; PDF p. 4, Figure 1

effect_estimate.comment: Although Section 2.3 mentions logistic regression at a 0.06 probability threshold, no regression coefficients or odds ratios are reported in the Results; quantitative findings are reported as descriptive percentages and bivariate correlation coefficients alongside qualitative institutional findings.
effect_estimate.value: Theoretical citywide drinking water access is 61% (~16 L/person/day), ranging from >60% connection rates in central planned neighborhoods (75% access in Ibanda, 6 days/week; 64% in Bagira, 5 days/week) to 45% in Kadutu (3 days/week) and <20% in peripheral informal neighborhoods; distance from the city center negatively correlates with drinking water service coverage (r = -0.42, p < 0.05). Informal settlements expanded from 15% of urban area (1980) to 85% (2024), while REGIDESO production (25,000–30,000 m3/day) falls below urban demand (70,000–72,000 m3/day; deficit >30,000 m3/day). Among surveyed households (N = 655), 45% rely on public standpipes (mean collection time 45 min), 32.8% use unimproved sources, and 43.7% use the parallel water market; 29.74% lack land titles (citing inheritance, procedure costs, and administrative burdens), 4.03% report parallel land titles, and untitled dwellings account for 68% of peripheral and 74% of informal-neighborhood homes where regular network connection is poor. Distance correlates strongly with collection time (r = 0.963) and moderately with waterborne disease occurrence (r = 0.582; collection time and disease r = 0.411; water price and disease r = -0.431).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the non-experimental mixed-methods design ceiling. Rated 2 because the study directly observes and documents the institutional, planning, and tenure mechanisms operating on water service through household surveys, institutional interviews, and field observations—including unsystematic land-title and building-permit procedures, lack of master-plan integration and inter-tier coordination, procedural costs and administrative burdens leaving 29.74% of households untitled, overlapping titles obstructing pipe rights-of-way, unregulated construction damaging REGIDESO pipes, and temporary disconnections of tenant homes over unpaid water bills.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines lack of formal land titles and unregistered plots (documentation), informal/customary/overlapping tenure and occupancy status (tenure), parallel titles, land conflicts, and pipe rights-of-way (property), master-plan non-integration, absence of functional zoning, and urban expansion beyond administrative/network boundaries (planning, zoning, service_area), unsystematic building-permit issuance (building_permit), cost of procedures and administrative burdens for titling (fees, procedural_steps), temporary disconnection for unpaid water bills among tenants (disconnection), neighborhood water committees (participation), and fragmented uncoordinated local/provincial/national governance (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).

sample_size.comment: Primary household survey sampled 655 households in 67 blocks across all 14 districts of Bukavu (mean household size 6.8). Supplemented by key-informant semi-structured interviews using 6 interview guides (exact interviewee N not reported), archival review of 7 urban plans, and multi-temporal GIS imagery. Secondary provincial/environmental health records cited in Section 3.5 cover 104 water samples (2025) and 1,732 confirmed cholera cases (2024).
sample_size.value: 655 households across 67 blocks in 14 districts (household survey); semi-structured interviews using 6 interview guides with REGIDESO officials, municipal authorities, and state technical services (exact interviewee N not reported); 5 Landsat imagery years (1984, 1989, 2000, 2011, 2024) and 1 Pléiades image; 7 historical urban planning documents (1927–2021)

study_design.comment: Combines quantitative household survey data (N = 655 households; descriptive statistics and correlation analysis; logistic regression is mentioned in Section 2.3 at p < 0.06, though no regression coefficients or odds ratios are reported in Results) and multi-temporal remote sensing/GIS modeling with qualitative semi-structured interviews of institutional officials, direct field observation, and archival planning analysis.
